knowledge_point.title: Using the Double-Angle Formula to Simplify Expressions

question.:question/problem:
Express

$$
2\cos^{4}\left(\frac{6\pi}{11}\right)-2\sin^{4}\left(\frac{6\pi}{11}\right)
$$

as a single trigonometric ratio.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Use the difference of squares, then the Pythagorean identity.

$$
\begin{aligned}
&2\cos^{4}\left(\frac{6\pi}{11}\right)-2\sin^{4}\left(\frac{6\pi}{11}\right) \\
&=2\left(\cos^{2}\left(\frac{6\pi}{11}\right)-\sin^{2}\left(\frac{6\pi}{11}\right)\right) \\
&\qquad\cdot\left(\cos^{2}\left(\frac{6\pi}{11}\right)+\sin^{2}\left(\frac{6\pi}{11}\right)\right)
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\cos^{2}\left(\frac{6\pi}{11}\right)+\sin^{2}\left(\frac{6\pi}{11}\right)=1$, this reduces to

$$
2\left(\cos^{2}\left(\frac{6\pi}{11}\right)-\sin^{2}\left(\frac{6\pi}{11}\right)\right).
$$

Recall the **double-angle formula for cosine**:

$$
\cos^2 x-\sin^2 x=\cos(2x).
$$

Substitute $x=\frac{6\pi}{11}$ and double the angle:

$$
\begin{aligned}
&2\left(\cos^{2}\left(\frac{6\pi}{11}\right)-\sin^{2}\left(\frac{6\pi}{11}\right)\right) \\
&=2\cos\left(2\cdot \frac{6\pi}{11}\right) \\
&=2\cos\left(\frac{12\pi}{11}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$

Only the angle doubles; the common coefficient stays outside the cosine.
